clinicalPearls: CLN5 disease is a variant late-infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis first delineated in Finnish families but now recognised worldwide.

Onset is typically a little later than classic late-infantile (CLN2) disease, opening with motor clumsiness and concentration difficulty in mid-childhood, then visual failure, myoclonus, ataxia and progressive dementia.
It is caused by biallelic variants in CLN5, which encodes a soluble lysosomal glycoprotein, so it is not one of the enzyme-deficiency NCL subtypes.
Early pigmentary retinopathy and visual loss are consistent features, in contrast to adult Kufs-type NCLs in which the retina is spared.
Brain MRI shows progressive cerebellar and cerebral atrophy, hypointense thalami and periventricular white-matter change.
Electron microscopy of stored material shows mixed inclusions, with fingerprint, curvilinear and rectilinear profiles rather than a single pattern.
Because there is no biochemical enzyme marker, diagnosis rests on molecular genetic testing rather than a leukocyte enzyme assay.
Storage material is rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, as in most non-enzymatic NCLs.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN5 disease is an autosomal recessive neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in CLN5 on chromosome 13q, which encodes CLN5, a soluble, heavily glycosylated lysosomal protein. Long regarded as functionally enigmatic, CLN5 is increasingly implicated in lysosomal lipid handling, including a proposed role in the metabolism of bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate, a lipid central to intralysosomal membrane digestion. Deficient CLN5 function disturbs lysosomal homeostasis and leads to progressive intraneuronal accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin storage material that, as in most non-enzymatic NCLs, is rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase. The consequence is widespread neurodegeneration with prominent cortical, cerebellar and retinal neuronal loss, producing the combination of dementia, motor decline, myoclonus, ataxia and visual failure. A Finnish founder allele accounts for most cases originally described in Finland, but pathogenic variants and disease occur worldwide.
additionalDifferentials: CLN8 variant late-infantile NCL and Northern epilepsy
Other progressive myoclonic epilepsies (Lafora disease, Unverricht-Lundborg disease, MERRF)
Late-infantile onset lysosomal disorders such as juvenile GM2 gangliosidosis
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing (CLN5 sequencing, NCL gene panel or exome sequencing)
Brain MRI for cerebellar and cerebral atrophy and thalamic signal change
EEG including photic stimulation, seeking a photoparoxysmal response at low flash rates
Electroretinography and formal ophthalmological review for retinal degeneration
Electron microscopy of skin or conjunctival biopsy showing mixed fingerprint, curvilinear and rectilinear profiles (now second-line)
Targeted exclusion of enzyme-deficient NCLs (PPT1, TPP1, cathepsin D) when the genotype is uncertain
redFlags: New visual failure with pigmentary retinopathy in a child whose motor and cognitive skills are regressing
Loss of previously acquired developmental milestones
Rapidly progressive ataxia and gait deterioration
reference.prognosis: CLN5 disease is relentlessly progressive, with loss of independent mobility, vision, speech and swallowing over years and death commonly in later childhood to adolescence. No disease-modifying therapy is licensed; management is supportive, although gene-directed approaches are under investigation.
pitfalls: Attributing early clumsiness or inattention to a behavioural or learning problem, delaying diagnosis.
Expecting a single ultrastructural inclusion type; CLN5 shows mixed profiles.
Searching for an enzyme deficiency; CLN5 is not enzyme-based and needs genetic confirmation.
Assuming it is a Finnish-only disease; CLN5 occurs worldwide.
Offering cerliponase alfa, which is specific to CLN2 and does not treat CLN5.
management: No licensed disease-modifying therapy exists, so provide coordinated supportive care, with gene-directed approaches available only within research settings
Control seizures and myoclonus with antiepileptic drugs, avoiding agents that aggravate myoclonus
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy and antispasticity management for progressive motor decline and ataxia
Arrange ophthalmology and low-vision support for pigmentary retinopathy and visual failure
Support nutrition and swallowing with gastrostomy feeding as bulbar function declines
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology, rehabilitation, palliative care and educational support
Offer genetic counselling, carrier testing and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
